'And the prince Mastema came and said before God: Behold, Abraham loves Isaac his son, and he delights in him above all things else; bid him offer him as a burnt-offering on the altar, and Thou wilt see if he will do this command, and Thou wilt know if he is faithful in everything wherein Thou dost try him' — the Akedah RE-FRAMED with Mastema as the accuser-instigator (parallel to Job 1-2's Satan-as-accuser). Tewahedo Akedah-theology preserves this Jubilees re-framing: the test originates in Mastema's challenge, but God permits it for Abraham's vindication. This protects God's absolute goodness while preserving the narrative of testing.

'And I stood before him, and before the prince Mastema, and the Lord said: Bid him not to lay his hand on the lad, nor to do anything to him, for I have shown that he fears the Lord' — Jubilees uniquely makes the angel of presence (not the Lord directly) the one who stays Abraham's hand, with the angel positioned BETWEEN Abraham and Mastema. The Tewahedo Akedah ikon tradition depicts this positioning literally: the angel between Abraham and an accusing figure, with the divine voice from above. The angel-of-presence Christological identification (a long Tewahedo patristic tradition reads the angel-of-presence as the pre-incarnate Word) makes the Akedah scene Christological even in its OT form.

'And Abraham called that place The Lord hath seen, so that it is said in the mount the Lord hath been seen — that is Mount Zion' — Jubilees explicitly identifies the Akedah mountain (Moriah) with Mount Zion (parallel to 2 Chr 3:1's Temple-mount identification). The Tewahedo eucharistic tradition draws this canonical identification into liturgical theology: every altar is mystically the Akedah mount AND the Temple mount AND Calvary AND the heavenly Zion. The fourfold identification (Moriah-Zion-Calvary-Heavenly-Zion) is preserved in Tewahedo Anaphora prayers and is the canonical anchor for the doctrine that 'the altar is in heaven and on earth at once.'

'And he observed this festival every year, seven days with joy, and he called it the festival of the Lord, according to the seven days during which he went and returned in peace. And accordingly has it been ordained and written on the heavenly tablets regarding Israel and its seed that they should observe this festival seven days with the joy of festival' — Abraham institutes a seven-day Akedah-commemoration festival, written on the heavenly tablets. Tewahedo liturgical historiography recognizes this as an Akedah-anniversary observance distinct from Pascha proper but liturgically connected. The seven-day duration and the joy-character (despite the sober content) prefigures the Tewahedo Holy-Week-into-Easter pattern: sober commemoration culminating in resurrection joy, all within one continuous festal week.
